rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden inhabitants say this in response to the angels’ greetings.
rows.anchor: These are the words of the inhabitants of the Garden in response to the greetings from the angels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s Promise includes the return of all human beings to Him, whether they are destined for Heaven or Hell.
rows.anchor: His Promise refers to that given to all human beings in 10:4, whether they are destined for Heaven or for Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers scoff at the true promise and challenge when it will occur, as several verses record.
rows.anchor: God’s Promise is true, a promise at which the disbelievers scoff in several verses, saying, When will this promise come to pass

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the promise also specifically includes the promises made to believers about abiding in blissful Gardens.
rows.anchor: more specifically to the various promises given to the believers, as in v. 20 as well as 31:8–9

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous inherit Paradise and the earth; inheriting the earth means they may settle wherever they wish.
rows.anchor: which can be understood to mean that they may do with it as they please and, in their own words, settle wheresoever we will.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels bearing or near the Throne supplicate for believers in 40:7–8; those near the Throne may be the angels encircling it here.
rows.anchor: those who bear the Throne and those who dwell nigh unto it (40:7), the latter of whom may be the same as those mentioned here, supplicate God saying,

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The final praise may be uttered by the angels or by God Himself.
rows.anchor: This final Praise be to God is uttered by the angels or by God Himself (IK).

rows.speaker: IK, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: Commentators infer that creation begins and ends with God’s praise, since this account closes with praise and creation opens with it.
rows.anchor: light, 6:1; IK, Q, Ṭs); they take this to imply that creation begins and ends with God’s praise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bearers of the Throne are eight angels, as stated in 69:17.
rows.anchor: Those who bear the Throne are eight angels, as in 69:17

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bearers may be the same angels who encircle the Throne in 39:75 or a distinct group among them.
rows.anchor: These may be the same as the angels encircling all around the Throne (39:75) or a distinct group among them.

rows.speaker: Ṭb
rows.claim: The Throne is where God’s Commands and Decrees issue and from where He directs the cosmos.
rows.anchor: the meaning of the Throne, from which God’s Commands and Decrees issue and from which He directs the cosmos (Ṭb)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The prayers of the highest angels show the difference between believers and disbelievers and reassure the Prophet and his followers amid disbelievers’ disputes.
rows.anchor: show the great difference between the believers and the disbelievers, whose fate is mentioned in the previous verse (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scripture attests that God encompasses all things in mercy and in knowledge.
rows.anchor: That God encompasses all things in Mercy is attested in 7:156; that He encompasses all things in knowledge is also attested in 6:80

rows.speaker: R, Ṭb
rows.claim: Some interpret the sentence’s structure to mean that God’s Mercy precedes or outstrips His Knowledge.
rows.anchor: Some understand the structure of this sentence to indicate that God’s Mercy precedes or outstrips His Knowledge (R, Ṭb)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The priority of divine Mercy is a principle in Islamic metaphysics and cosmology.
rows.anchor: for the priority and principiality of God’s Mercy in Islamic metaphysics and cosmology

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the angels seek forgiveness for believers; elsewhere they seek forgiveness for people on earth.
rows.anchor: Here the angels seek forgiveness for those who believe; elsewhere they seek forgiveness for those on earth (42:5).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse connects intercession and seeking forgiveness with 2:48 and 2:255, and shielding from Hellfire with 44:56.
rows.anchor: For further discussion of seeking forgiveness for others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Day of Resurrection, all humanity comes from its graves and gathers on one plain.
rows.anchor: When all human beings come forth from their graves and are gathered on a single plain

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: One reported interpretation has all those gathered answer that sovereignty belongs to God, the One, the Paramount.
rows.anchor: all who are gathered will respond, It is God’s, the One, the Paramount (Q, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IK, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: Another interpretation has God Himself answer the question about sovereignty.
rows.anchor: or it is God Himself who answers the question (IK, Q, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istaqāmū (“stand firm”) is related to the phrase for performing prayer and to the Quranic idea of the straight path.
rows.anchor: Stand firm translates istaqāmū, a word closely related to the common phrase “perform the prayer”

rows.speaker: IJ, IK, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: One interpretation is continuing to affirm God’s oneness without turning to other gods.
rows.anchor: those who continue to say that God is One and do not turn to other gods (IJ, IK, Q, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IJ, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: Another interpretation is remaining obedient to God and maintaining religious obligations.
rows.anchor: those who remain obedient to God and maintain their religious obligations (IJ, Q, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: Another interpretation is remaining sincere and doing good deeds until death.
rows.anchor: those who remain sincere and continue to perform good deeds until death (IJ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: These readings converge on obedience to God in belief, speech, and action.
rows.anchor: all indicate maintaining obedience toward God in belief, speech, and action (Q).

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet taught that those who affirm God as Lord and persist until death are among the steadfast, since many who said it later disbelieved.
rows.anchor: It is reported that the Prophet recited this verse and then said, “Some people have said it [“Our Lord is God”], and then most of them disbelieved.

rows.speaker: Aj, IJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The angels’ descent is interpreted as occurring at death or when people are drawn from their graves.
rows.anchor: either at the moment of death, at the moment they are drawn from their graves (Aj, IJ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Aj, Ṭs
rows.claim: Another interpretation places the angels’ descent at the Resurrection, when humanity is gathered.
rows.anchor: or at the Resurrection, when all human beings are gathered (Aj, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The descent can also refer to angels helping people in this world by inspiring good, opening their hearts, and aiding religious matters.
rows.anchor: It can also be understood as a reference to angels descending upon people in this world, inspiring them to do good

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: “Fear not” concerns what is to come, while “nor grieve” concerns what has passed.
rows.anchor: Fear not refers to what is to come, while nor grieve refers to what has passed (IJ, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: My
rows.claim: The promise of the Garden echoes the description of the righteous workers’ reward in 3:136.
rows.anchor: And rejoice in the Garden, for Blessed indeed is the reward of the workers [of righteousness]! (3:136; My)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awliyāʾ can mean protectors, friends, or allies; here the angels both guard believers and love them.
rows.anchor: Protectors translates awliyāʾ (sing. walī), which can also mean“friends” or “allies.”

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: The angels’ protection continues in the Hereafter until believers enter Paradise, comforting them in their graves and when the trumpet is blown.
rows.anchor: they will watch over the believers until the believers enter Paradise (IJ, Ṭs), providing them comfort while they are in their graves

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The angels escort believers across the traverse from the Judgment plain to the Garden.
rows.anchor: escorting them across the traverse that leads from the plain of Judgment to the Garden (IK).

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī and al-Maybudī
rows.claim: They interpret angelic protection in this world as realization of gnosis and in the Hereafter as obtaining forgiveness.
rows.anchor: al-Qushayrī and al-Maybudīprovide several interpretations for this verse

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī and al-Maybudī
rows.claim: They interpret it in this world as contentment with the Decree and in the Hereafter as meeting in the Abode of Subsistence.
rows.anchor: al-Qushayrī and al-Maybudīprovide several interpretations for this verse

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī and al-Maybudī
rows.claim: They interpret it in this world as faith and in the Hereafter as forgiveness.
rows.anchor: al-Qushayrī and al-Maybudīprovide several interpretations for this verse

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī and al-Maybudī
rows.claim: They interpret it in this world as love and in the Hereafter as nearness.
rows.anchor: al-Qushayrī and al-Maybudīprovide several interpretations for this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that believers receive whatever they desire in the Hereafter is discussed at 56:20–24.
rows.anchor: For the idea that the believers will have whatsoever they desire in the Hereafter, see commentary on 56:20–24.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This protection may allude to the salvific standing of all revealed religions, as in 2:62 and 5:59.
rows.anchor: That such protection is afforded those who say, “Our Lord is God,” then stand firm could also be an allusion to the salvific nature of all revealed religions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s control of the sea lets ships travel with sufficient wind and protects travelers from too little wind or destructive excess; this is a sign of His mercy.
rows.anchor: That God subjugates the sea and allows ships to travel upon it without hindering their travel by withholding the wind or causing travelers to perish by sending too much wind

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The ships also symbolize human frailty, while the metaphor presents God giving or withholding provision as He knows is best for each person.
rows.anchor: the ships also indicate the frailty of the human condition, and the metaphor relates to the manner in which God bestows and withholds provision in accord with what He knows is best for each individual (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patient people benefit from seeing affliction as too much or too little wind, and thankful people benefit from ease of travel.
rows.anchor: Those who are patient when affliction befalls them, which could be seen as the times of too much or too little wind, and who are thankful when able to travel with ease, benefit from reflecting upon these signs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People perish and are punished because of their own iniquities; God does not wrong them, while they wrong themselves.
rows.anchor: people only perish and are punished because of their own iniquities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The symbolism of seafaring also applies to the spiritual life.
rows.anchor: For more on the symbolism of seafaring as it pertains to the spiritual life, see 30:46c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zukhruf is a Makkan surah believed to follow al-Shūrā directly.
rows.anchor: l-Zukhruf is a Makkan sūrah, believed to have been revealed directly after Sūrah 42, al-Shūrā

rows.speaker: Āl, IJ
rows.claim: Some authorities hold that verse 45 is from the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: some maintain that v. 45 is from the Madinan period (Āl, IJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah takes its name from the mention of gold ornaments in verse 35.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the mention of gold ornaments in v. 35.

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The opening discussion of the Quran and the Mother of the Book may continue the preceding surah’s statement that revelation was made a light of guidance.
rows.anchor: some propose that in discussing the nature of the Quran and the Mother of the Book in the first verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah opens with a brief discussion of revelation.
rows.anchor: After opening with a brief discussion of revelation (vv.2–5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It next cites the fate of earlier communities who rejected their prophets.
rows.anchor: the sūrah cites the fate of previous communities who rejected the prophets sent to them (vv. 6–8)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah challenges the worldview of the Makkan idolaters, answering their objections and addressing forms of disbelief.
rows.anchor: The first half of the sūrah responds to different objections that the Makkan idolaters are reported to have posed to the message of the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One objectionable belief is assigning partners to God.
rows.anchor: such as assigning partners to God (vv. 15)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah rebukes the claim that angels are God’s female offspring.
rows.anchor: claiming that the angels are God’s female offspring (v. 19)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah addresses the claim that God willed idolaters to worship angels.
rows.anchor: saying that God willed for them to worship the angels (v. 20)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idolaters object that the Quran should have been revealed to someone of high social standing.
rows.anchor: claiming that the Quran should have been revealed to someone who was already of high social standing (v. 31)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah rebukes likening the religious role of idols to Jesus’ role in Christianity.
rows.anchor: likening the place of deities in their religion to the place of Jesus in Christianity (vv.57–58)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A major theme is the mistaken use of ancestral tradition as a measure of truth.
rows.anchor: claiming to follow the tradition of one’s forefathers (vv. 22–25)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another mistaken measure of truth is treating worldly wealth as an indicator of one’s true station.
rows.anchor: seeing the wealth of this world as an indicator of one’s true station (vv.31–36)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham exemplifies opposition to his people’s attachment to their forefathers.
rows.anchor: Abraham is cited as an example of someone who opposed his people’s attachment to their forefathers (vv. 26–28)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idolaters’ opposition to the Prophet is likened to Pharaoh and his notables opposing Moses.
rows.anchor: the opposition of the idolaters to the Prophet is likened to the opposition of Pharaoh and his “notables” toward Moses (vv.46–56)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah firmly rebukes the attempt to liken idol worship to Christian worship of Jesus.
rows.anchor: The idolaters’ attempt to liken their worship of idols to the Christian worship of Jesus is also firmly rebuked (vv.57–65).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An extended contrast of believers’ and disbelievers’ fates in the Hereafter follows these examples.
rows.anchor: there is an extended contrast of the fate of believers and disbelievers in the Hereafter (vv. 66–78)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah then challenges the idolaters’ belief system again.
rows.anchor: followed by another challenge to the belief system of the idolaters (vv. 79–87)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah closes by instructing the Prophet to remain calm amid the disbelievers’ opposition.
rows.anchor: the sūrah ends with an injunction to the Prophet to remain calm in the face of the disbelievers’ opposition to his message (vv. 88–89).
